[&_blockquote_p::after]:hidden","children":[["$","p","p-0",{"children":"Preston Paul Meeres, widely known by his stage name \"The Sepia Valentino\" or \"The Brown Valentino,\" was a pioneering Bahamian dancer, musician, nightclub owner, and cultural ambassador. During the heights of the Harlem Renaissance and the golden age of European cabaret, Meeres brought Caribbean-infused rhythms, jazz-era tap, and theatrical dance to international audiences, performing alongside legends like Josephine Baker and Cab Calloway. Upon his return to the Bahamas, he established \"Chez Paul Meeres,\" a legendary entertainment complex that served as Nassau's premier cultural hotspot and a launching pad for future generations of Bahamian artists."}],"\n",["$","h3","h3-0",{"children":"Early Life in Green Turtle Cay and Grant's Town"}],"\n",["$","p","p-1",{"children":"Preston Paul Meeres was born on August 13, 1902, in the picturesque settlement of New Plymouth on Green Turtle Cay, Abaco, Bahamas. His parents, Paul Aitken Meeres and Victoria Russell-Gilbert, were of modest means, and his early childhood was spent amidst the marine-centered life of the Abaco Cays. When he was still a young boy, the family relocated to Nassau, settling in the historic \"Over-the-Hill\" community of Grant’s Town."}],"\n",["$","p","p-2",{"children":"Grant’s Town was the cultural heartbeat of Black Nassau. It was a place where West African traditions, Junkanoo rhythms, and local folklore merged to form a rich cultural tapestry. Growing up in this environment, young Paul was exposed to the vibrant sounds of the Goombay drum, the whistle, and the concertina. Although he had no formal training in dance or music, he possessed an innate sense of rhythm and a magnetic stage presence that drew the attention of neighbors and peers."}],"\n","$Ld","\n","$Le","\n","$Lf","\n","$L10","\n","$L11","\n","$L12","\n","$L13","\n","$L14","\n","$L15","\n","$L16","\n","$L17","\n","$L18","\n","$L19","\n","$L1a","\n","$L1b","\n","$L1c","\n","$L1d","\n","$L1e","\n","$L1f","\n","$L20","\n","$L21","\n","$L22","\n","$L23","\n","$L24","\n","$L25","\n","$L26"]}]]}],"$L27","$L28",false]}],"$L29"]}]
8:["$","script","script-0",{"src":"/_next/static/chunks/2uyb8-0enc77-.js","async":true}]
9:["$","script","script-1",{"src":"/_next/static/chunks/2z-jpqdx1wamk.js","async":true}]
a:["$","script","script-2",{"src":"/_next/static/chunks/08pctmd9kh4qh.js","async":true}]
b:["$","$L2a",null,{"children":["$","$2b",null,{"name":"Next.MetadataOutlet","children":"$@2c"}]}]
d:["$","h3","h3-1",{"children":"Emigration and the Great Migration: The Contract"}]
e:["$","p","p-3",{"children":"In 1920, at the age of eighteen, Meeres joined the thousands of Bahamians participating in \"The Contract\" (commonly referred to by Bahamians as \"The Project\" or \"The Recruitment\"). This was an agreement between the colonial government of the Bahamas and agricultural employers in the United States to recruit seasonal farm laborers. Meeres traveled to the United States to work in the agricultural fields of the American South."}]
f:["$","p","p-4",{"children":"However, the grueling labor of the farms could not contain his artistic ambitions. The early 1920s coincided with the Great Migration of African Americans from the South to northern cities, and Meeres soon made his way to New York City. Settling in Harlem, he entered a community that was undergoing a historic cultural explosion known as the Harlem Renaissance."}]
10:["$","h3","h3-2",{"children":"Stardom in the Harlem Renaissance: \"Meeres & Meeres\""}]
11:["$","p","p-5",{"children":"In Harlem, Meeres pivoted entirely to the entertainment industry, teaching himself to sing, play instruments, and master the intricate steps of tap and ballroom dance. In 1925, he married Thelma Dorsette, a Brooklyn-born performer of Bahamian and Jamaican heritage. Recognizing their shared talent, they formed a professional dance partnership called \"Meeres & Meeres\"."}]
12:["$","blockquote","blockquote-0",{"children":["\n",["$","p","p-0",{"children":"\"They were the Negro Astaires. Their feet moved with the speed of lightning and the grace of swans, bringing a distinct Caribbean warmth to the stages of Harlem.\""}],"\n"]}]
13:["$","p","p-6",{"children":["Billed as \"the Negro Astaires\" or \"the Sepia Astaires,\" Meeres & Meeres became one of the most celebrated dance acts of the Harlem Renaissance. They performed at the iconic Cotton Club and Connie’s Inn, sharing the stage with jazz greats like Duke Ellington and Louis Armstrong. In 1929, the duo reached the pinnacle of Broadway success, appearing in the musical revue ",["$","em","em-0",{"children":"Hot Chocolates"}],", which featured music by Fats Waller and launched the international career of Cab Calloway. Their style was a unique fusion of elegant ballroom dancing, high-energy tap, and syncopated rhythms that reflected their Caribbean heritage."]}]
14:["$","h3","h3-3",{"children":"Solo Stardom in Europe and \"The Sepia Valentino\""}]
15:["$","p","p-7",{"children":"Following a divorce from Thelma in 1930, Paul Meeres embarked on a solo career, touring internationally. He traveled to Europe, where he found an artistic climate that was highly receptive to Black entertainers. In Paris, Meeres became a sensation, performing at the world-famous Folies Bergère. He worked closely with Josephine Baker, the undisputed queen of Parisian cabaret, and toured Spain, Italy, and Germany."}]
16:["$","p","p-8",{"children":"It was during his European tours that Meeres earned the moniker \"The Sepia Valentino\" or \"The Brown Valentino\". Audiences and critics compared his suave, romantic stage presence and striking good looks to the silent film icon Rudolph Valentino. Meeres was known for his impeccable style, often performing in tailored tuxedos or elaborate silk costumes, and his dances became celebrated for their blend of sensuality, precision, and theatricality."}]
17:["$","h3","h3-4",{"children":"Return to Nassau and the Vision of \"Chez Paul Meeres\""}]
18:["$","p","p-9",{"children":"By 1939, with the outbreak of World War II threatening Europe, Meeres decided to return to his homeland. He arrived in Nassau with a wealth of international experience, a substantial sum of money, and a vision to transform the Bahamian entertainment landscape. At the time, Nassau was a segregated city where Black Bahamians were barred from major hotels and clubs."}]
19:["$","p","p-10",{"children":["Meeres purchased property in his childhood neighborhood, at the corner of Fleming Street (which would later be colloquially known as \"Paul Meeres Corner\") and Market Street in the \"Over-the-Hill\" area of Grant's Town. There, he established ",["$","strong","strong-0",{"children":"Chez Paul Meeres"}],", a multifaceted entertainment complex that included a nightclub, a hotel, and the Paul Meeres Movie Theatre."]}]
1a:["$","h3","h3-5",{"children":"The Chez Paul Meeres Phenomenon"}]
1b:["$","p","p-11",{"children":"Chez Paul Meeres quickly became Nassau's premier night spot and a symbol of Black economic and cultural success. The club’s interior was designed to match the glamour of the Parisian and Harlem cabarets Meeres had performed in, featuring a polished wooden dance floor, tropical decor, and a state-of-the-art sound system."}]
1c:["$","p","p-12",{"children":"Despite the racial segregation of Nassau's main tourist areas, Chez Paul Meeres became a crossover success. It attracted wealthy international tourists, British colonial officials, and Hollywood celebrities who traveled \"Over-the-Hill\" to experience authentic Bahamian music, dance, and hospitality. Stars such as Elizabeth Taylor and Ava Gardner were known to have frequented the club during their visits to the Bahamas."}]
1d:["$","p","p-13",{"children":"The entertainment at the club was legendary. Meeres hosted elaborate floor shows that featured fire dancers, steel pan bands, calypso singers, and goombay musicians. He also performed himself, delighting patrons with his signature dances and bringing a touch of European sophistication to the Nassau stage."}]
1e:["$","h3","h3-6",{"children":"Mentorship and the Discovery of \"Peanuts\" Taylor"}]
1f:["$","p","p-14",{"children":"Beyond its commercial success, Chez Paul Meeres served as an important training ground and launchpad for local Bahamian talent. Meeres was a generous mentor who recognized the potential of young Bahamians who had talent but lacked opportunities."}]
20:["$","p","p-15",{"children":"The most famous example of Meeres' mentorship was his discovery of John Berkley \"Peanuts\" Taylor. As a young boy, Taylor would sing and dance on the streets of Nassau to earn money. One evening, Meeres spotted the young boy performing outside his club. Impressed by his raw talent and rhythm, Meeres brought Taylor inside, gave him a job, and personally trained him in the arts of showmanship, drumming, and dance. Taylor would go on to become \"Peanuts\" Taylor, one of the Bahamas' most legendary goombay drummers, entertainers, and cultural icons, carrying the torch of Bahamian cabaret around the world."}]
21:["$","h3","h3-7",{"children":"Twilight Years, the Burning of the Tropicana, and Death"}]
22:["$","p","p-16",{"children":["By the late 1950s, the political and social landscape of the Bahamas was shifting. The rise of the Progressive Liberal Party (PLP) under leaders like ",["$","$L2d","a-0",{"slug":"lynden-pindling","href":"/profiles/lynden-pindling","children":"Lynden Pindling"}]," was challenging the dominance of the white merchant oligarchy, and labor unions led by ",["$","$L2d","a-1",{"slug":"randol-fawkes","href":"/profiles/randol-fawkes","children":"Randol Fawkes"}]," were mobilizing the working class."]}]
23:["$","p","p-17",{"children":"In 1957, after nearly two decades of running Chez Paul Meeres, Paul Meeres Sr. leased the club to a Swedish couple, who renamed the venue \"The Tropicana\". However, the new chapter was short-lived. In 1958, during a period of intense labor strikes and political tension in Nassau, the club burned to the ground under suspicious circumstances. The loss of the physical structure marked the end of an era for Nassau's nightlife."}]
24:["$","p","p-18",{"children":"Paul Meeres Sr. passed away on September 13, 1962, in Nassau at the age of sixty. His legacy, however, was carried on by his son, Paul Keith Meeres Jr. (1925–1986), who became a celebrated professional dancer in his own right, performing in the United States and internationally."}]
25:["$","h3","h3-8",{"children":"Legacy and Cultural Impact"}]
26:["$","p","p-19",{"children":"Preston Paul Meeres was a pioneer who helped shape modern Bahamian show business. By bridging the worlds of the Harlem Renaissance, European cabaret, and Bahamian folk traditions, he proved that Caribbean culture had a place on the world's most prestigious stages. Through Chez Paul Meeres, he created a space where Black artists could perform with dignity, and where Bahamian music and dance were celebrated as world-class art forms. He remains a national cultural icon, remembered for his elegance, his artistry, and his unwavering belief in the power of Bahamian talent."}]
27:["$","$Lc",null,{"title":"Learn about the legacy of Paul Meeres","url":"https://caribbeanlegacyarchive.com/profiles/paul-meeres"}]
